text: Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, combines a retriever with a language model. The retriever fetches relevant passages from a knowledge base, and the language model conditions its answer on those passages. This grounds responses in external facts and reduces hallucinations compared to relying on the model's parametric memory alone.
title: What is retrieval-augmented generation

text: Dense retrieval encodes queries and documents into fixed-size vectors with an embedding model, then ranks documents by cosine similarity or dot product. Dense search captures semantic similarity, so a query about automobiles can match a document about cars even when no words overlap.
title: Dense vector search

text: BM25 is a classic sparse retrieval function based on term frequency and inverse document frequency. It rewards documents that contain rare query terms many times, with saturation and length normalization. BM25 is exact and fast, but it cannot match synonyms or paraphrases.
title: BM25 keyword search

text: Hybrid search combines sparse keyword retrieval such as BM25 with dense vector retrieval. The two ranked lists are fused, often with reciprocal rank fusion, so documents that score well on both lexical and semantic signals rise to the top. Hybrid search is the default choice for production RAG systems.
title: Hybrid search

text: Reciprocal rank fusion, or RRF, merges ranked lists without needing comparable scores. Each document gets a score of 1 / (k + rank) from every list it appears in, and the scores are summed. The constant k, usually 60, dampens the influence of very high ranks.
title: Reciprocal rank fusion

text: A cross-encoder reranker takes a query-document pair and outputs a single relevance score, attending jointly over both texts. It is more accurate than bi-encoder similarity but too slow to run over a whole corpus, so it is used to rerank the top candidates from a cheaper first-stage retriever.
title: Cross-encoder reranking

text: Milvus is an open-source vector database for storing and searching embedding vectors at scale. It supports approximate nearest neighbor indexes such as HNSW and IVF, scalar filtering, and hybrid search over dense and sparse vectors. Milvus Lite runs the same engine embedded in a single file with no server.
title: Milvus vector database

text: HNSW, hierarchical navigable small world, is a graph-based approximate nearest neighbor index. Vectors become nodes in layered graphs, and search walks greedily from the top layer down. It offers excellent recall and low latency, and is the most popular index for vector databases.
title: HNSW index

text: Chunking splits long documents into retrievable pieces. Fixed-size chunking is simple but can cut sentences in half. Sentence-aware and semantic chunking keep coherent ideas together, and adding small overlaps preserves context across chunk boundaries. Chunk size trades off precision against context richness.
title: Chunking strategies

text: Embedding models map text to vectors where similar meanings sit close together. Bi-encoder models like MiniLM and BGE are trained with contrastive objectives on query-document pairs. Choosing an embedding model tuned for retrieval, rather than a generic sentence model, usually improves RAG quality more than any index tuning.
title: Embedding models

text: Retrieval is evaluated with ranking metrics: recall at k measures how many relevant documents appear in the top k, mean reciprocal rank rewards putting the first relevant document early, and nDCG discounts relevance by position. A small labeled set of queries with known relevant documents is enough to compare naive and hybrid pipelines.
title: Evaluating retrieval

text: Query expansion rewrites the user's question before retrieval. Techniques include generating hypothetical answer passages, extracting key terms with a language model, or simply lowercasing and stemming. Expansion helps when the query vocabulary differs from the document vocabulary.
title: Query expansion

text: LangChain provides retriever abstractions that wrap vector stores, including Milvus, with a common interface. An EnsembleRetriever combines multiple retrievers with weighted reciprocal rank fusion, and a ContextualCompressionRetriever adds a reranking or compression step on top of base retrieval.
title: LangChain retrievers

text: Agentic RAG gives a language model tools such as a retriever and lets it decide when to search, what to search for, and whether the evidence is sufficient. Instead of a fixed retrieve-then-generate pipeline, the agent loops: search, read, reason, and search again until it can answer or gives up.
title: Agentic RAG

text: Graph RAG builds a knowledge graph of entities and relationships from the corpus, then retrieves connected subgraphs for a query. It shines for multi-hop questions that require joining facts across documents, such as who acquired whom and when, where plain chunk retrieval misses the links.
title: Graph RAG

text: Retrieved documents can contain malicious instructions that hijack the language model, a risk known as indirect prompt injection. Defenses include keeping retrieved text in a clearly delimited context, instructing the model to treat it as untrusted data, and filtering or quarantining suspicious passages before generation.
title: Prompt injection in RAG

text: Grounding checks that every claim in a generated answer is supported by the retrieved evidence. A common pattern is to have the model cite chunk identifiers inline, then verify each citation with a second pass. Answers with unsupported claims are repaired or withheld instead of shown to the user.
title: Citations and grounding

text: Production RAG must fit a latency budget: embedding the query, first-stage retrieval, reranking, and generation each add milliseconds. Typical tricks are smaller embedding models, quantized indexes, reranking only the top 20 candidates, and streaming the answer token by token so the user sees progress early.
title: Latency budgets
